title: The 4-20 mA current loop
summary: A 4-20 mA transmitter represents its measuring range as a current. The live zero at 4 mA lets the PLC tell a real zero from a broken wire.

sections.heading: Why current, and why 4 mA
sections.body: A current is the same everywhere in a series loop, so cable resistance and moderate noise do not change the value. Starting at **4 mA** instead of 0 mA gives a **live zero**: 0 mA can only mean a fault (broken wire, missing supply), while 4 mA means the lower end of the range. Two-wire transmitters are even powered from the loop current.

sections.heading: NAMUR NE 43 signal levels
sections.body:
The NAMUR recommendation NE 43 separates measurement from failure information:

| Current | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| 3.8 to 20.5 mA | measurement information (including small under- and overrange) |
| at or below 3.6 mA | failure information (low) |
| at or above 21.0 mA | failure information (high) |

A transmitter that follows NE 43 saturates at 3.8 and 20.5 mA during normal operation and drives the failure current when its self-diagnostics detect a fault.

sections.heading: Converting current to percent
sections.body: `percent = (I - 4 mA) / 16 mA * 100`. 12 mA is therefore 50 %, 8 mA is 25 %. PLC Lab's level transmitter saturates at the NE 43 limits; a broken loop delivers 0 mA, which the analog input reports as wire break when diagnostics are enabled.

facts.label: NE 43 failure levels
facts.value: at or below 3.6 mA, at or above 21.0 mA
